note: Read, p. 43: 'His house, at 1905 Prairie Avenue, deserves a place in the first rank ... It is a large and roomy mansion, standing by itself, with abundant breathing-room on the southern side, where a spacious lawn and scattered shade-trees suggest green fields and the natural attractions of the country.' Pp. 43-44: 'Mr. Field's house is of red pressed brick, with trimmings of light sandstone, three stories in height, with main entrance in the center of the west front, at the head of a broad flight of granite steps, a high porte-cochère on the northern side, and a fine large conservatory on the southern. Stables and other out-buildings are in the rear, on the side nearest the lake.' Pp. 44-45, the reception-room: 'A window opens into the conservatory, rich in rare plants and bright flowers, in the center of which a fountain plays ceaselessly into its bronze basin.' P. 47, the dining-room: 'Glass doors out of this room lead into the conservatory, and a window looks out upon the spacious lawn.' The text is an interior survey; these few sentences are all it says of the grounds. It describes the house about twenty years before the scene date.
what_it_supplies: an open south yard by 1883-84: 'a spacious lawn and scattered shade-trees' on the southern side
the conservatory on the south side, opening from the reception-room and the dining-room, with plants and an indoor fountain
the stables and other out-buildings at the rear, on the lake (east) side
the porte-cochere on the north side and the entrance in the centre of the west front, up granite steps
red pressed brick with light sandstone trim, three storeys
what_it_does_not_supply: the yard in 1904: it is twenty years earlier
the number, species or places of the shade-trees
any flower bed, walk or fence outdoors: the flowers it names are inside the conservatory
any dimension of the lawn, the conservatory or the stables
